claims.text: At stage-4 docs/design/system-design-method.md is the team's method for every new design problem; its refund example looks back at the stage-3 refund work and decides nothing again.

refund-requirements.md YC-1..YC-6: a signed-in customer requests a refund for their own paid order; others' orders refused; full amount; status shown, no second request; cancelled + email on success; rejected requests listed for staff with the gateway's reason.
ADR 0003 records splitting Payments into its own service (DonHang.Payments, database donhang_payments), joined to the API by a saga over messages.
refund-requirements.md has an out-of-scope list (partial refunds, shipped orders, cash on delivery, staff creating requests for customers).
Step 1's output in the method: scope, key operations, quality attribute scenarios, constraints, assumptions with who confirms them, and a ranked list of drivers.
A feature list rarely changes a design's shape; answers about how many, what may be stale or late, what must never happen and what keeps working when a dependency fails usually do.

YC-7 rules out calling the gateway inside the customer's request; instead the API records the request and answers (202), and a Payments background job calls the gateway later, joined by the saga of ADR 0003.
Under YC-9, every resend to the gateway reuses the same key refund-<id>, so an order is never refunded twice.

Method 29-44: step 1 asks by group (who/key operations; how many users, ops/s, data, busiest hour; stale or late, how long; never happen; what runs when a dependency fails; constraints: team, deadline, ADRs, compliance); an unanswered question becomes an assumption with a confirmer by role.
refund-requirements.md's open-questions table names, for each question, who answers it and by when.

Method lines 46-59 rank three refund drivers: YC-7, YC-9, and the gateway API key with money rows as the most sensitive part (citing ADR 0003's context); YC-1..YC-6 add features without changing shape; YC-10 follows from YC-7 and YC-9.

ADR 0003's context names YC-7, YC-9, YC-10 and the sensitivity of the gateway API key and the money rows (the payments table); it chose a separate service so they sit in one service of their own; consequences add a service, compensating steps, old table (N2).
ADR 0003's consequences: the order and the refund request agree only after a while (order refunding while the Payments row is pending).
No YC in refund-requirements.md states the gateway-key sensitivity, and none states how many refunds to expect.

Trade-offs: starting from features finds drivers late; answering every question first starts the design late; shape questions with assumptions and a ranked list cost a session and upkeep but pay back when a part is costly to undo.

An unknown volume becomes an assumption confirmed by the product owner; only a different size (thousands of refunds/s, not a fraction of one) sends the sketch back; a day limit on refunds is a feature rule near YC-1; rank a long unordered list before design.
refund-requirements.md has an open question on how many days after payment the gateway allows a refund, answered by the gateway provider, asked by the product owner.
The method's refund estimate assumes 1% of orders refunded, about 1,000 refund requests on the busiest day, about 120 in its busiest hour, and comes to about 0.03 refund requests per second.
Designing for the maximum when a number is unknown adds parts no driver asks for; requirements pull against each other and the ranking decides which wins.

Try it grouping: YC-1..YC-6 who/key operations; YC-7, YC-10 dependency fails; YC-9 never happen; YC-8 never happen or, by its accounting reason, compliance; the third driver is a security concern from ADR 0003's context, not refund-requirements.md.
